A classify() that returns on the first typed match inside a joined error's Unwrap() is picking scheduler order, not severity — do not read it as 'most severe wins'

top_rules: Treat ESRCH from the post-Wait group sweep as success, never an error — it is kill(2)'s documented response to an already-empty group.
The sweep is reuse-safe exactly while a target descendant is alive: the kernel keeps a pgid attached (unrecyclable) as long as any group member exists, leader-reaped or not.

Add SysProcAttr.Pdeathsig: SIGKILL to the SDK's direct child on Linux as a SHOULD companion to the sweep — it's the only mechanism covering the SDK's own process being SIGKILLed/OOM-killed, since no Go code runs to perform the sweep then.

Never set Pdeathsig without pairing it with runtime.LockOSThread() around Start-through-Wait — the ecosystem's own shipped fix (containerd's vendored go-runc) for the golang/go#27505 thread-vs-process footgun.

Pdeathsig exists only on syscall.SysProcAttr for linux and freebsd (verified from exec_linux.go/exec_freebsd.go vs exec_libc2.go/exec_bsd.go/exec_libc.go); GOOS=darwin go vet ./... proves its absence elsewhere.
Scope the Pdeathsig SHOULD to Linux only, not the stdlib's wider linux||freebsd — no fleet target or exemplar, including go-runc itself, exercises FreeBSD.
Never add a delay or retry between Cmd.Wait() returning and the sweep's Kill(-pgid, SIGKILL) call — any extra step only widens the narrow already-empty-group coincidence window.
pidfd (Go 1.23+) fixes the single-pid wait/kill race but has no group-scoped analogue — never credit it with making the group sweep safe; that safety comes from process-group membership semantics.
surprises: An initial corpus re-grep for Pdeathsig wrongly reported zero hits; the corrected unfiltered re-grep found 10, including two real containerd production sites (pkg/sys/unshare_linux.go, core/mount/mount_idmapped_utils_linux.go).

containerd's vendored go-runc already ships the exact runtime.LockOSThread mitigation for golang/go#27505, citing it by name and warning GOMAXPROCS=1 can hang — this dive adopted that shape rather than inventing one.

The Linux kernel keeps a process-group's numeric id unrecyclable as long as ANY member (even a lone surviving descendant, with the leader already reaped) exists — the sweep's safety comes from group membership, not from timing relative to Wait.
go-runc itself gates Pdeathsig support to plain linux (command_other.go: //go:build !linux), narrower than the Go stdlib's actual linux||freebsd availability — no exemplar anywhere exercises FreeBSD.

Go's own os/pidfd_linux.go source comment explicitly names CL 23967 and confirms the single-pid wait/kill race is real, but pidfd has no group-scoped analogue, so it can't rescue the numeric -pgid sweep.

The camelCase grep for unpaired Pdeathsig usage false-positives on a variable literally named usePdeathsig, since Go identifiers give grep -w no word boundary there — worth flagging as a reading-heuristic limitation.

Run the go-upgrade procedure in strict order: release notes -> GODEBUG diff (in-workspace and GOWORK=off) -> go/toolchain bump -> go fix -> stdversion -> golangci pin/config -> GOEXPERIMENT audit -> full gate; never rely on dependabot for a toolchain-only bump.
surprises: asynctimerchan is a removed GODEBUG as of Go 1.27: on the 1.27.1 toolchain, a go1.22-line AND a go1.23-line module both measure unbuffered timer channels (cap 0) — the release note's per-module-line gate only held on toolchains 1.23-1.26; setting the env var is now a fatal build error, not a revert.

In workspace mode a member module's own godebug default=… line in go.mod is silently and completely ignored; only go.work's godebug block is consulted. GOWORK=off flips this exactly — verified live with go list -f '{{.DefaultGODEBUG}}'.

io/ioutil's own deprecated wrappers (TempFile, ReadFile, etc.) carry //go:fix inline directives in stdlib source itself — the generic inline fixer, not a dedicated ioutil fixer, migrates them, and it is file-go-line-gated: confirmed declining live on google/go-cmp (go1.21) and stretchr/testify (go1.17).

dependabot-core will never open a PR whose sole purpose is bumping the go/toolchain line (open issue #13520); it only lets that line move as an incidental side effect of an unrelated dependency bump, since a 2024-era bug that reverted the Go tool's own edit was fixed by PR #12228.

go fix's own driver (via go vet -vettool=$(go tool -n fix)) diverges from the x/tools modernize library used in the prior wave's census: go1.27's go fix gained atomictypes/embedlit/slicesbackward/unsafefuncs and dropped fmtappendf, so the two 'modernization census' tools are not interchangeable.

minmax, rangeint and stringsseq all verified to decline their risky case by construction (NaN, body-mutated loop var, reused split slice) rather than merely being 'safe on average' — none of the 459 fresh-census diagnostics across 12 exemplars was a case where the self-limit should have fired but didn't.

top_rules: P0 resolved: default jsonv2-backing in Go 1.27.1 changes zero bytes of v1 encoding/json output — verified byte-identical vs GOEXPERIMENT=nojsonv2 across dup-names, invalid UTF-8, case-mismatch, large-int-into-any, omitempty, MarshalIndent, HTML escaping.
A go-1.26-floor library needs one golden fixture for v1 encoding/json output, not two per toolchain leg, and must never import encoding/json/v2 or jsontext directly while that floor stands.
No GODEBUG restores v1 json behaviour — jsonv2 is a build-wide GOEXPERIMENT, not a go-line-keyed runtime toggle, and the nojsonv2 escape hatch itself is announced for future removal.
omitempty and omitzero are not interchangeable on a slice: omitempty drops both nil and []T{}; omitzero drops only nil and keeps []T{} as [] — a mechanical rename silently changes envelope shape.

Map iteration order into any observable output has zero linter/vet coverage in golangci-lint 2.14.0 or staticcheck/gocritic (enable-all) — the only check is `go test -run <golden> -count=5` watched for a flip.

time.Time == is false after a JSON round-trip of the same instant (monotonic reading lost), and a map[time.Time] lookup with that value silently misses; no analyzer catches it — use .Equal(), never a mixed-provenance time.Time map key.
Decoding into any/map[string]interface{} silently loses integer precision above 2^53 with err==nil; Decoder.UseNumber() fixes it and is unaffected by the jsonv2 backend.

rand.Seed is a fully-covered no-op (SA1019, watched red/green via both staticcheck and golangci-lint on a planted fixture); math/rand/v2 has no global Seed at all, only local rand.New(rand.NewPCG(...)).
surprises: staticcheck's SA6003 does NOT catch byte-vs-rune string slicing (it targets a different, performance-only []rune-before-range pattern) — the map's classification of M-A-09 as staticcheck-covered was wrong; it stays a pure reading heuristic.
gocritic with every check enabled (`enable-all: true`) finds zero issues on a time.Time == time.Time comparison — no linter catalogue in scope covers this footgun at all, not even opportunistically.

google/go-github@48d0a668cde8 already declares go 1.26.0 with hand-written (Un)MarshalJSON methods — a live exemplar sitting exactly on the SDK's own floor scenario, and its custom Marshaler/Unmarshaler dispatch is unaffected by the jsonv2 backend.

GOEXPERIMENT and GODEBUG are fully separate mechanisms: GODEBUG can be keyed to an importing module's go line (like containermaxprocs), but GOEXPERIMENT cannot — it is fixed for the whole build, so no library's go.mod can ever protect its consumers from a jsonv2 toolchain default.

The go1.27 notes explicitly flag GOEXPERIMENT=nojsonv2 itself as temporary ('expected to be removed in a future release'), meaning the escape hatch this whole P0 investigation revolves around has its own expiration risk.

stdlib uuid and google/uuid v1.6.0 are fully format-and-parse-compatible in both directions including braced/URN/bare-hex forms — a real network `go get` round-trip test, not just a doc read, found zero incompatibility.

top_rules: Never add a new pkg/ directory; go.dev's own layout doc never mentions pkg/ at all -- check a new repo's diff for an added top-level pkg/.

Exported interface with exactly one implementation and no documented reason is the defect, not producer-side interfaces generally (measured ~55/45 producer/consumer split) -- ireturn watched red/green.

Options are a decision procedure (positional / config struct / func-typed-with-error-on-conflict / interface-typed), not one winning pattern -- grpc-go's 100% interface-typed DialOption proves a naive func( grep alone misjudges half the ecosystem.

Self-deprecation is Deprecated: plus //go:fix inline (1.26+); go fix -diff exits 1 on a pending rewrite and 0 once callers migrate -- watched end-to-end on a real fixture.

apidiff always exits 0 (report-only, confirmed on 3 diff pairs); the real CI gate is gorelease, whose exit code is major-version-dependent by design -- identical removed-method change exits 0 on a v0 module and 1 on a v1+ module, confirmed via a local file-based module proxy.

go vet's composites check catches an unkeyed literal of another module's exported struct only across module boundaries, not same-package -- watched red/green on a real 3-module fixture with a replace directive.

No linter exists for slice/map aliasing at a boundary (M-D-07) or embedding leaks (M-D-13) -- both are reading heuristics; the aliasing row got a behavioral-proof test pair instead of a red/green analyzer signal.

A fleet library's major-version strategy (stay at v1 forever vs. periodic /vN) is a one-time stated project decision, not decided per release -- grpc-go and go-github both succeed with opposite strategies; gorelease enforces whichever is chosen.
surprises: apidiff never fails on its own -- it exits 0 unconditionally even reporting an incompatible removal; only gorelease's exit code is major-version-conditional, and that had to be proven by hand-building a local file-based Go module proxy since the fixture modules have no real VCS/proxy presence.

go.dev/doc/modules/layout never mentions pkg/ at all, not even to reject it -- the community's pkg/-vs-internal/ debate is entirely absent from Go's own canonical layout doc.

exhaustive tolerates a default: clause as long as every real case is also listed -- it does not treat default's presence as automatically satisfying exhaustiveness, contrary to a plausible assumption.

Getting gorelease to run at all against fixture modules required constructing a hand-rolled Go module proxy directory (@v/<ver>.info/.mod/.zip) since gorelease resolves its -base version through normal module resolution, not a local directory or git tag.

top_rules: Every constructed *http.Client sets Timeout>0; never http.DefaultClient/Get/Post/Head — belt-and-suspenders beyond GO-CONC's context rule (watched: hangs at 1.5s without Timeout, fails at ~300ms with it)

bodyclose fails the <=1 FP/10k-LOC bar on regclient (~92% FP, wrapper-close-elsewhere shape) but 2 real leaks survive hand-reading (BlobDelete, BlobGet's error branch) — GO-NET's close-and-drain MUST rests on a reading heuristic; bodyclose stays SHOULD-only on direct net/http code

Bound every response body with io.LimitReader(resp.Body, n+1) before io.ReadAll — unbounded ReadAll pulled a full 1GiB body into memory in 1.24s; the +1 read distinguishes truncation from a body that fit

net/http's client body Close() auto-drains up to 256KiB (maxPostHandlerReadBytes) before giving up on reuse — closing without draining only churns connections once the unread remainder exceeds that threshold (watched via httptrace)
Retry only 429/503/5xx-except-501 and only idempotent methods unless an idempotency key exists — hashicorp/go-retryablehttp's DefaultRetryPolicy ignores method entirely and will retry a POST on a 500

Parse Retry-After with both delay-seconds and HTTP-date forms — regclient's time.ParseDuration(header+"s") silently drops the HTTP-date form to a 0 delay (confirmed by fixture); go-retryablehttp gets both right

Default http.Client strips Authorization on redirect keyed on url.Hostname() only (port-blind) and asymmetrically (dest-subdomain-of-origin keeps it, reverse strips it) — confirmed on 1.27.1 by fixture

vet's hostport analyzer only fires when Sprintf-built host:port reaches net.Dial in the SAME function — an identical bug split across a helper is silently missed (confirmed: crossfunc.go not flagged, samefunc_bad.go flagged)
surprises: net/http's client-side body Close() silently auto-drains up to 256KiB (maxPostHandlerReadBytes, server.go:1164) of an unread body so the connection can still be pooled — 'close without draining' is only actually harmful above that threshold, not always

Two httptest.Server instances both bound to 127.0.0.1 on different ports are NOT a cross-host redirect to net/http's Authorization-stripping check, because it compares url.Hostname() only (port-excluded) — had to rewrite the Location header to 'localhost' to get a genuine cross-host test

The redirect-Authorization stripping rule is directionally asymmetric: origin->subdomain keeps credentials, subdomain->origin strips them, which is backwards from how many registry/CDN layouts are actually arranged

hashicorp/go-retryablehttp's DefaultRetryPolicy has no method/idempotency check at all — it will retry a POST on a bare 500 exactly like a GET, a live divergence from RFC 9110 in the ecosystem's most-cited Go retry library

bodyclose's hand-classified false-positive rate on regclient is ~92%, but the 2 survivors are genuine: BlobDelete leaks on every path, and BlobGet leaks only on its non-200 error branch after correctly transferring ownership on the success path — a defect shape invisible to both the linter and a quick read
gosec G107's own documentation example is itself the rule's false-positive shape (a hardcoded var string flagged as tainted input)

top_rules: MUST: never treat a partial (non-EOF) read as verified — verify.ReadCloser/go-digest only check at io.EOF, so a stream must be drained to completion before trust
MUST: compare digest and size by exact value only, never by prefix/substring — a wrong-size payload can share an arbitrary digest prefix with the real one
MUST: validate digests against the full OCI grammar plus per-algorithm exact length/lower-case-hex; a well-formed-but-unknown algorithm is a distinct, milder error than a malformed one

MUST: stage every content-addressed blob write in a uniquely-named temp file and rename into place; never os.Create/O_TRUNC directly at the final path (oras-go's pushFile shape corrupts under concurrent writers)

SHOULD: a verified content-addressed store needs no cross-process lock for concurrent same-digest ingest — atomic rename of independently-verified temp files is safe by construction; a lock only serializes shared partial-ingest state, which staging removes the need for
MUST: sweep orphaned *.tmp on store open and never rename a partially-verified temp file — a SIGKILL mid-ingest must leave the final path absent, watched behaviorally

MUST: every on-disk format a Go tool owns carries an explicit version/magic marker checked on open, refusing a NEWER-than-supported version explicitly, not just an older one — precedented by OCI's oci-layout imageLayoutVersion and containerd's schemaVersion/dbVersion migration table

MUST: resolve credentials via config.json credHelpers/credsStore and the docker-credential-<suffix> get protocol; treat a configured helper's exec failure as a hard error, never silently as 'no credentials' — errcheck/gosec catch only the adjacent ignored-JSON-error half, not the swallowed-exec-error half
surprises: opencontainers/go-digest, the reference Go digest library, implements only sha256/sha384/sha512 — it does NOT support blake3 even though image-spec registers it, so a client needs its own hasher for blake3

A content-addressed store needs NO cross-process lock for correctness under concurrent same-digest ingest — verified content + atomic rename makes the race harmless by construction; containerd's own Ref-keyed lock is in-process-only and solves a different problem, not this one
containerd's local content store treats a rename-target collision as ErrAlreadyExists (terminal success), never as an overwrite — most callers swallow it

oras-go's credential-store API is mid-migration in the read exemplar: module path has moved to /v3 and it now carries a NamespaceMatcher interface plus Hierarchical matching for containers-auth.json (Podman/Buildah) compatibility, beyond the v2 shape the brief named

errcheck/gosec DO catch an ignored json.Unmarshal error sitting right next to the naive credential resolver's real bug, but neither catches the actual bug (swallowing exec.Command's error as 'no credentials') — a lint hit is a good trigger to read the function by hand, not proof it's fine

The deterministic two-writer splice (channel-forced interleaving, not a timing race) reproduced exactly as predicted: os.Create truncates the SAME inode a concurrent writer is mid-write on, leaving a file matching neither writer's content at the trusted final path

rule_ids: GO-NET-01 — Construct every http.Server with ReadHeaderTimeout > 0; never call http.ListenAndServe/ListenAndServeTLS/Serve (gosec G112/G114)
GO-NET-02 — Never reference http.DefaultClient, including DefaultClient.Do, which noctx accepts
GO-NET-03 — Derive every Transport from http.DefaultTransport.(*http.Transport).Clone(); never write a bare &http.Transport{} literal; registry clients raise MaxIdleConnsPerHost
GO-NET-04 — Build host:port with net.JoinHostPort; check with a grep, since vet hostport is blind to DialContext
GO-NET-05 — Every credentialed client sets a CheckRedirect with a hop cap and an https->http refusal, and binds credentials to the destination origin (scheme, host, port)
GO-NET-06 — Build clients in one constructor with a stall bound: Client.Timeout for API clients; ResponseHeaderTimeout plus a context deadline or idle watchdog for blob streams
GO-NET-07 — Bound every network body: LimitReader(max+1) with reject on the client, MaxBytesReader in handlers
GO-NET-08 — Parse Retry-After in both forms (ParseInt, then http.ParseTime) and cap the honoured delay
GO-NET-09 — Close every response on every return path, error branches included, or transfer ownership to a returned io.Closer
GO-NET-10 — Never drain an untrusted body unbounded; stdlib already drains <=256 KiB on Close
GO-NET-11 — Retry only transport errors, 408, 429 and 5xx except 501, on idempotent or replayable requests, with capped jittered backoff
GO-NET-12 — Drain a verifying reader to io.EOF and check its error before using any byte; check size, then digest
GO-NET-13 — Parse digests strictly (lower-hex, exact length) and compare them whole, never by prefix
GO-NET-14 — Stage blobs via CreateTemp in the store dir, verify, then rename; an existing target means success; no lock as the fix; sweep own temp files on open
GO-NET-15 — Version every owned on-disk format and refuse a newer version on open
GO-NET-16 — Resolve credentials via credHelpers, then credsStore, then auths; a configured helper's failure is a hard error
GO-NET-17 — CLIs wrap go-containerregistry with a context deadline and a cloned transport; the SDK imports no OCI library
GO-NET-18 — Set User-Agent <tool>/<version> on every outbound request
GO-NET-19 — Servers stop via signal.NotifyContext plus Shutdown with a bounded grace period

Wave-2's 'G101 fires only at package scope, never local :=' is WRONG - re-verified on 10 planted variants: G101 fires at any scope on vendor-shaped or high-entropy literals; the real gap is low-entropy dictionary secrets and values built via concatenation or a second variable, at ANY scope.

Secrets must be compared with crypto/subtle.ConstantTimeCompare, never == ; no gosec rule or linter catches == comparisons - confirmed 0 issues on a planted violation, closed with a grep heuristic instead.

html/template is MUST for any HTML-bound template; text/template must never reach an HTTP response - no analyzer catches this (0 issues on fixture); closed with a two-step grep (text/template import intersect http.ResponseWriter reference).

unsafe, //go:linkname and cgo are forbidden without a merged ADR; enforcement is a grep since gosec G103 did not fire on any planted unsafe.Pointer/String/SliceData call in golangci-lint 2.14.0 despite matching its own rule source.

Wrap r.Body in http.MaxBytesReader before json.NewDecoder or ParseMultipartForm; a smaller ParseMultipartForm(maxMemory) argument alone does NOT silence gosec G120 - verified still-red without MaxBytesReader, green only with it.
A struct field named like a secret reaching json.Marshal fires gosec G117; json:"-" silences it - verified red/green.
surprises: Wave 2's G101 'package-scope only' claim is false for gosec's current source and golangci-lint 2.14.0: G101 registers on local AssignStmt exactly like package-scope ValueSpec; the real gap is entropy/value-shape (dictionary secrets, concatenated or indirected literals), not scope - re-verified on 10 planted variants.

gosec G120 (unbounded ParseMultipartForm) fires unconditionally on any call regardless of the maxMemory argument passed; a smaller maxMemory does not silence it, only wrapping r.Body in http.MaxBytesReader first does - matches G120's own doc comment but contradicts the intuitive 'just pass a smaller number' fix.

top_rules: GO-REL-01 MUST: -trimpath on every release build — omitting it leaked the absolute build path into the binary and broke bit-reproducibility (watched red/green)
GO-REL-02 MUST: CGO_ENABLED=0 explicit in build/release jobs — unset resolves to 1 whenever gcc is on PATH, silently producing a dynamically-linked binary (watched red/green)
GO-REL-04 MUST: cross-compile with CGO_ENABLED=0 — CGO_ENABLED=1 to a non-native GOARCH dies in the assembler (watched: exit 1 vs exit 0)
GO-REL-05 MUST: stamp semver via -ldflags -X AND VCS metadata via runtime/debug.ReadBuildInfo together, never one alone (10/35 corpus precedent)
GO-REL-07 MUST-NOT: release version must never carry a +dirty suffix — CI fails if go version -m shows it (watched red/green)
GO-REL-09 SHOULD: bake -X main.date from CommitDate, never wall-clock Date — same-path builds seconds apart produced different sha256 otherwise (watched)

GO-REL-10 SHOULD: run govulncheck -mode=binary on the unstripped artifact before stripping — stripped build over-reported 4 findings vs 1 on the identical reachable CVE (independently re-measured, matches GO-MOD-13)

GO-REL-08 SHOULD: pin archive mtimes via goreleaser mod_timestamp — it is a post-build os.Chtimes call, not a go-build flag, and covers a second reproducibility layer the binary-level flags don't touch
surprises: mod_timestamp is not a go-build/GOFLAGS knob at all — it's goreleaser's own post-build os.Chtimes() call on the artifact file (confirmed by reading goreleaser's own source, internal/gio/chtimes.go / internal/builders/base/build.go), so a binary can be byte-reproducible while its release archive is not, and vice versa is impossible to fix without it

-s -w does not touch the embedded runtime/debug.BuildInfo at all — go version -m was byte-identical between stripped and unstripped twins; only govulncheck -mode=binary's reachability precision degrades, and it over-reports (4 vs 1 finding), it does not miss the real reachable CVE

CGO_ENABLED is legitimately scoped per-build-id, not per-repo: sigstore/cosign sets CGO_ENABLED=1 at the top level for one pkcs11/pivkey variant but overrides it back to 0 inside its plain linux build entry — a single goreleaser file can need three different CGO_ENABLED postures

Go 1.25 added a real, currently-open regression/behavior change (golang/go#74763): a repo with more than one independent VCS root now hard-fails buildvcs with 'multiple VCS detected', and a nested-module-without-root-go.mod topology silently degrades from a real pseudo-version to '(devel)' — neither existed under Go 1.24

os/user and net both degrade gracefully to pure-Go with CGO_ENABLED=0 (identical uid output either way) — the real hazard isn't that these packages 'need' cgo, it's that CGO_ENABLED left unset defaults to 1 on any host with a C compiler on PATH, producing an unintentionally dynamic binary

goreleaser's own unpinned defaults (GOARCH: [386, amd64, arm64], GOARM: [6], GOAMD64: [v1]) are narrower than actual corpus practice (windows+arm64 in 9/11 configs), and GOARM/GOAMD64 pins never appear standalone — always alongside an already-broad arm matrix tied to a real hardware target

The stdlib leak detector's own call site cancels out of the before/after diff for free (stripping file:line frames makes both snapshots' self-referential frame identical), so no special-casing of the detector's own goroutine was needed.

Go's automatic 'all goroutines are asleep' deadlock detector actively interfered with the first SIGQUIT fixture attempt — it exited the process before SIGQUIT could be sent, because a real full-deadlock (no runnable goroutine) self-reports; a realistic hung-service fixture needed a heartbeat goroutine to suppress that and force a genuine SIGQUIT read.

goroutineleak was already experimental in Go 1.26, not new in 1.27 as the topic map's framing implied; only the GA promotion (and deletion of the goroutineleakprofile GOEXPERIMENT flag) is new in 1.27.

go_sdk.from_file's toolchain line beats its go line for SDK version selection — measured both ways (1.27.1 vs 1.27.0) on the same fixture.

io/process-group-sweep: The Linux kernel keeps a process-group's numeric id unrecyclable as long as ANY member (even a lone surviving descendant, with the leader already reaped) exists — the sweep's safety comes from group membership, not from timing relative to Wait.

language/era-and-modernizers: asynctimerchan is a removed GODEBUG as of Go 1.27: on the 1.27.1 toolchain, a go1.22-line AND a go1.23-line module both measure unbuffered timer channels (cap 0) — the release note's per-module-line gate only held on toolchains 1.23-1.26; setting the env var is now a fatal build error, not a revert.

language/era-and-modernizers: In workspace mode a member module's own godebug default=… line in go.mod is silently and completely ignored; only go.work's godebug block is consulted. GOWORK=off flips this exactly — verified live with go list -f '{{.DefaultGODEBUG}}'.

language/era-and-modernizers: io/ioutil's own deprecated wrappers (TempFile, ReadFile, etc.) carry //go:fix inline directives in stdlib source itself — the generic inline fixer, not a dedicated ioutil fixer, migrates them, and it is file-go-line-gated: confirmed declining live on google/go-cmp (go1.21) and stretchr/testify (go1.17).

language/era-and-modernizers: dependabot-core will never open a PR whose sole purpose is bumping the go/toolchain line (open issue #13520); it only lets that line move as an incidental side effect of an unrelated dependency bump, since a 2024-era bug that reverted the Go tool's own edit was fixed by PR #12228.

language/era-and-modernizers: go fix's own driver (via go vet -vettool=$(go tool -n fix)) diverges from the x/tools modernize library used in the prior wave's census: go1.27's go fix gained atomictypes/embedlit/slicesbackward/unsafefuncs and dropped fmtappendf, so the two 'modernization census' tools are not interchangeable.

language/era-and-modernizers: minmax, rangeint and stringsseq all verified to decline their risky case by construction (NaN, body-mutated loop var, reused split slice) rather than merely being 'safe on average' — none of the 459 fresh-census diagnostics across 12 exemplars was a case where the self-limit should have fired but didn't.

language/stdlib-semantics: GOEXPERIMENT and GODEBUG are fully separate mechanisms: GODEBUG can be keyed to an importing module's go line (like containermaxprocs), but GOEXPERIMENT cannot — it is fixed for the whole build, so no library's go.mod can ever protect its consumers from a jsonv2 toolchain default.

language/stdlib-semantics: The go1.27 notes explicitly flag GOEXPERIMENT=nojsonv2 itself as temporary ('expected to be removed in a future release'), meaning the escape hatch this whole P0 investigation revolves around has its own expiration risk.

language/stdlib-semantics: stdlib uuid and google/uuid v1.6.0 are fully format-and-parse-compatible in both directions including braced/URN/bare-hex forms — a real network `go get` round-trip test, not just a doc read, found zero incompatibility.

network/http-client-server: net/http's client-side body Close() silently auto-drains up to 256KiB (maxPostHandlerReadBytes, server.go:1164) of an unread body so the connection can still be pooled — 'close without draining' is only actually harmful above that threshold, not always

network/http-client-server: Two httptest.Server instances both bound to 127.0.0.1 on different ports are NOT a cross-host redirect to net/http's Authorization-stripping check, because it compares url.Hostname() only (port-excluded) — had to rewrite the Location header to 'localhost' to get a genuine cross-host test

network/http-client-server: The redirect-Authorization stripping rule is directionally asymmetric: origin->subdomain keeps credentials, subdomain->origin strips them, which is backwards from how many registry/CDN layouts are actually arranged

network/http-client-server: hashicorp/go-retryablehttp's DefaultRetryPolicy has no method/idempotency check at all — it will retry a POST on a bare 500 exactly like a GET, a live divergence from RFC 9110 in the ecosystem's most-cited Go retry library

network/http-client-server: bodyclose's hand-classified false-positive rate on regclient is ~92%, but the 2 survivors are genuine: BlobDelete leaks on every path, and BlobGet leaks only on its non-200 error branch after correctly transferring ownership on the success path — a defect shape invisible to both the linter and a quick read
network/http-client-server: gosec G107's own documentation example is itself the rule's false-positive shape (a hardcoded var string flagged as tainted input)

network/registry-client: opencontainers/go-digest, the reference Go digest library, implements only sha256/sha384/sha512 — it does NOT support blake3 even though image-spec registers it, so a client needs its own hasher for blake3

network/registry-client: A content-addressed store needs NO cross-process lock for correctness under concurrent same-digest ingest — verified content + atomic rename makes the race harmless by construction; containerd's own Ref-keyed lock is in-process-only and solves a different problem, not this one
network/registry-client: containerd's local content store treats a rename-target collision as ErrAlreadyExists (terminal success), never as an overwrite — most callers swallow it

network/registry-client: oras-go's credential-store API is mid-migration in the read exemplar: module path has moved to /v3 and it now carries a NamespaceMatcher interface plus Hierarchical matching for containers-auth.json (Podman/Buildah) compatibility, beyond the v2 shape the brief named

network/registry-client: errcheck/gosec DO catch an ignored json.Unmarshal error sitting right next to the naive credential resolver's real bug, but neither catches the actual bug (swallowing exec.Command's error as 'no credentials') — a lint hit is a good trigger to read the function by hand, not proof it's fine

network/registry-client: The deterministic two-writer splice (channel-forced interleaving, not a timing race) reproduced exactly as predicted: os.Create truncates the SAME inode a concurrent writer is mid-write on, leaving a file matching neither writer's content at the trusted final path

security/untrusted-input-and-crypto: Wave 2's G101 'package-scope only' claim is false for gosec's current source and golangci-lint 2.14.0: G101 registers on local AssignStmt exactly like package-scope ValueSpec; the real gap is entropy/value-shape (dictionary secrets, concatenated or indirected literals), not scope - re-verified on 10 planted variants.

security/untrusted-input-and-crypto: gosec G120 (unbounded ParseMultipartForm) fires unconditionally on any call regardless of the maxMemory argument passed; a smaller maxMemory does not silence it, only wrapping r.Body in http.MaxBytesReader first does - matches G120's own doc comment but contradicts the intuitive 'just pass a smaller number' fix.

security/untrusted-input-and-crypto: gosec G103 (audit use of unsafe) did not fire on any planted unsafe.Pointer/unsafe.String/unsafe.SliceData call under golangci-lint 2.14.0's bundled gosec, despite G103's own upstream source registering exactly those call identifiers - an unexplained vendored-build vs upstream-source discrepancy.

security/untrusted-input-and-crypto: Caddy's own HTTP template middleware deliberately uses text/template (not html/template) for response bodies, documenting the real risk as server-side template injection (untrusted template content) rather than missing output-escaping - html/template would not fix that risk either; Caddy's directory-listing handler separately uses text/template with correct manual per-sink escaping plus a CSP nonce as defense in depth.

security/untrusted-input-and-crypto: A 20-site classification of math/rand v1 production usage found zero real security-sensitive uses (all jitter/backoff, temp-filename disambiguation, or test/benchmark data) except one borderline case: a local dev/test OCI registry minting an upload-session ID with math/rand and returning it in a URL - low stakes only because it's a test fixture registry.
